title: Cleaning Science and a Safe Production Room

say: Welcome to Cleaning Science and a Safe Production Room, module 1 of this course.
Before you mix anything, learn why each product works, what sits in your store, and how to keep this room safe.

shots.label: Surfactant at work
say: Look at this greasy surface. Water alone can not move grease, because oil and water do not mix.
This spray carries a surfactant, a molecule with one end that loves water and one that loves oil.
As we wipe, the grease breaks into tiny droplets wrapped in surfactant, and they float away.

shots.label: pH paper strip

card.title: Match the dirt to the pH

say: Watch the strip change colour. We match it against the chart.
The pH scale runs from 0 to 14. Pure water is 7, neutral. Below 7 is acid, above 7 is alkaline.
Grease needs alkaline. A toilet ring needs acid. Germs need a disinfectant after cleaning.

shots.label: Time: contact before rinsing
say: See the timer running while the surface stays wet? Time is one of the four cleaning forces.
The others are chemistry, action like scrubbing, and temperature. If one goes down, another must go up.
When your toilet cleaner label says leave for 10 minutes, time is doing the work.

shots.label: Bleach and acid cleaner
shots.banner: Never mix bleach with acid or ammonia
say: These two bottles stay apart: bleach on one side, acid toilet cleaner on the other.
Bleach with acid releases chlorine gas. Bleach with ammonia releases toxic chloramine gases. Both harm eyes and lungs.

shots.label: Caustic soda (sodium hydroxide)
say: This white, flaky powder is caustic soda, which chemists call sodium hydroxide. It also comes as pearls.
It neutralises LABSA, the dark brown sulphonic acid, about 96% active, that becomes your main surfactant.
It is corrosive and heats up strongly in water.

shots.label: Checking a delivery
say: Every delivery goes on the scale. Bisi in Ibadan weighs her jerrycan of SLES 70%, which traders call texapon.
Full, it weighs 26.4 kg. The empty can weighs 1.4 kg, so she has 25.0 kg.
Ask suppliers for a safety data sheet and a certificate of analysis. No documents? Buy a little and mark it strength unknown.

shots.label: Four storage zones
say: Look at this shelf. Every container is closed and labelled, with a clear gap between groups.
Acids sit together: LABSA and citric acid. Alkalis sit together: caustic soda and soda ash. Bleach stays alone.
Isopropyl alcohol and fragrances go in a fourth spot, away from heat, sockets and any flame.

shots.label: Sealed, off the floor
say: Watch the lid going on tight. Caustic soda pulls water from the air and goes lumpy, so powders stay sealed and off the floor.
And please, never store any chemical in a water bottle, soft-drink bottle or food tub. People have drunk cleaning chemicals from familiar bottles.

shots.label: Goggles, gloves, apron
say: Here is your protection: closed splash goggles, thick rubber gloves and an apron, with long sleeves and closed shoes.
Sunglasses will not stop a splash from the side, and eyes cannot be replaced.

shots.label: One-way room layout
say: This mixing table sits by an open window, so fumes and dust move outside.
Materials move one way: store, weighing, mixing, resting and testing, filling, then the finished-goods shelf.
Nobody carries concentrate back past someone filling bottles, and clean water sits beside every splash point.

shots.label: Caustic soda INTO water
shots.banner: Never pour water onto caustic soda
say: Watch: the flakes go slowly into cold water, a little at a time, never the other way round. See the heat rising?
Use a heat-resistant plastic container, never aluminium, because caustic soda attacks it.
LABSA also goes into water, with stirring. And label every bucket, even if it is only for an hour.

shots.label: Running water and eye-wash
shots.banner: Rinse eyes and skin for at least 15 minutes
say: If something splashes your eye, rinse it under gently running clean water for at least 15 minutes, holding the eyelids open.
On skin, take off the wet clothing and rinse the same way. Never use vinegar to neutralise a splash.
If someone swallows a product, don't make them vomit. Rinse the mouth and get medical help at once, with the label.
You now know why products clean, how to store your materials, and how to protect yourself.
Go through the lessons below, then do the practice tasks: your dirt map, your raw-material register and your safety station photo.
